title: Why You're Tired, Stressed, And Not The Teacher You'd Like To Be e-to-be/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes a common trajectory in which early-year discipline gradually erodes into complacency around week three, colliding with students' own growing restlessness to produce what he calls "the perfect storm" of declining behavior and rising teacher stress. He offers seven additional reasons never to waver from a classroom management plan, covering how consistent enforcement protects against parent complaints, preserves student respect, reduces reliance on stressful persuasion and intimidation tactics, prevents teachers from becoming the resentful, stone-faced version of themselves they never wanted to be, and staves off classroom chaos. He closes with a direct call to action: regardless of how inconvenient or well things seem to be going in the moment, a broken rule should always be met with calm, assertive enforcement of the stated consequence.
points: A predictable "perfect storm" emerges around week three, when early teacher complacency meets rising student restlessness.
Consistent enforcement of a classroom management plan functions as an insurance policy against parent complaints.
Every unenforced consequence costs a teacher a layer of student respect and increases reliance on stressful persuasion tactics.
Abandoning a classroom management plan risks turning a teacher into the stone-faced, sarcastic figure they never wanted to become.
The article closes with a direct call to calmly and assertively enforce every broken rule, regardless of inconvenience.
quotes: By week three, you’re cruising. But then… slowly, imperceptibly, things start becoming routine, more day-to-day, and you become a wee bit complacent.
When your ever-so-slight complacency runs headlong into your students’ restlessness, it creates the perfect storm, one that builds slowly and ominously just out of your awareness.
A classroom management plan is an insurance policy against parent complaints; it's fair to all students.
For every time you fail to enforce a consequence (i.e., not doing what you said you’d do), you lose a layer of respect from your students.
Teachers who disregard their classroom management plan are the same teachers who find themselves being ‘that’ teacher—the one they never pictured themselves being: stone-faced, angry, sarcastic.
Your classroom will fall into chaos and disorder without a willingness to stick with the plan you agreed to on the first day of school year.
No matter how inconvenient it may seem at the time or how well things seem to be going… when a classroom rule is broken, calmly and assertively do what you said you would do… And enforce it.
